name: Quaternion
seoDesc: Quaternion: work out magnitude |q₁| from the real part and the i coefficient. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Quaternion calculator turns the real part and the i coefficient into magnitude |q₁|. It is built for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Quaternion calculator work?
sections.html:
The Quaternion calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports magnitude |q₁| in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the real part (a), the i coefficient (b), the j coefficient (c) and the k coefficient (d).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the Quaternion calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Magnitude |q₁|=(the square root of ((real part (a) ^ 2) + (the i coefficient (b) ^ 2) + (the j coefficient (c) ^ 2) + (the k coefficient (d) ^ 2)))
Magnitude |q₂|=(the square root of ((real part (e) ^ 2) + (the i coefficient (f) ^ 2) + (the j coefficient (g) ^ 2) + (the k coefficient (h) ^ 2)))
Axismag=(the square root of ((the x coordinate (xₐ) ^ 2) + (the y coordinate (yₐ) ^ 2) + (the z coordinate (zₐ) ^ 2)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take I want to find the set to product, Real part (a) = 10, The i coefficient (b) = 10 and The j coefficient (c) = 10. The calculator returns Magnitude |q₁| = 20, Magnitude |q₂| = 20 and Axismag = 17.3205.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Magnitude |q₁| = 20, Magnitude |q₂| = 20 and Axismag = 17.3205 should be roughly the size you expected from I want to find the set to product and Real part (a) = 10.

Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Angle, opening in degrees

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Quaternion calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Splitting a bill, a measurement or a shape problem between several people
  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the real part and the i coefficient — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Quaternion calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns magnitude |q₁|, derived from the real part and the i coefficient. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Quaternion calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the real part and the i coefficient, which is 13 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter angle (θ) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Angle (θ) opens in degrees and the chip beside it offers 12 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Magnitude |q₁| = 20. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Quaternion calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
